newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says Albanian PM must decide Berisha's fate.
newsitem.headline: Italy says Albanian PM must decide Berisha's fate.

text.p: Italy distanced itself on Saturday from embattled Albanian President Sali Berisha and said his fate was in the hands of Bashkim Fino, the new prime minister of the crisis-hit Balkan state.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was quoted in a press interview as saying it was up to Fino, a member of the main opposition Socialists and head of a new unity government, "to assess what Berisha's role might now be".

Fino had to decide whether Berisha's presence was "an obstacle to pacifying the country or not, whether his continuation in the role can be accepted at least to prepare elections or not," Dini told La Repubblica newspaper.

His remarks signalled that Italy, Albania's biggest economic partner and at the forefront of diplomatic efforts to resolve Albania's anarchy, no longer saw the rightist president as a key player in the country, diplomats said.

Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said Italy was taking a "highly neutral" line on whether Berisha should resign and noted that his departure could heighten tension in Albania's north, where support for him is strongest.
But a leading leftist Italian politician, Achille Occhetto, said the Albanian leader should follow what he interpreted as Dini's "advice" to quit.
"Dini's affirmation...is in itself diplomatically very important, it is almost a word of advice," Occhetto, chairman of the lower house foreign affairs commission, said.
"I believe the Albanian president could cooperate, could make a further effort by submitting his resignation and asking in return that the insurgents immediately surrender their arms."

The rebels, who control several southern towns, accuse Berisha of failing to control bogus pyramid schemes, in which many citizens poured their savings. Their collapse ignited unrest which has degenerated into armed insurrection.
Rome had been regarded as Berisha's closest contact in the European Union until this month's violence and lawlessness. He sent his son and daughter to safety in Italy on Thursday.
In the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, where EU foreign ministers were discussing the crisis, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said openly that Berisha should quit.

"I'm sure that if President Berisha were to step down that would in some ways improve the situation in Albania," said Petersen, whose country holds the chairmanship of the 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

A report for the OSCE by crisis mediator Franz Vranitzky said Berisha, all political parties and rebel committees share the same goal: the restoration of order and democracy and the holding of fresh elections.
But Dini said rebel representatives had told Vranitzky during talks on an Italian warship on Friday that while they supported Fino's government they wanted Berisha to go.
"The (rebel) committees said that they will hand in their weapons only after Berisha has resigned," he said.
Berisha, whose Democratic Party won a landslide in elections last year which international observers said were deeply flawed, has given no indication that he intends to resign.
His re-election to a second five-year term by parliament went ahead on March 3 as armed unrest sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid savings schemes engulfed the south.
He initially refused to form a new coalition government in response to the uprising but bowed to international pressure last weekend by agreeing to a deal with opposition parties.
Fino's government is meant to lead the country to internationally supervised early elections by June.
